This article applies `isoformic` to Oxford Nanopore long-read cDNA sequencing of 22Rv1 prostate cancer cells treated with lorecivivint, an inhibitor of the CDC-like kinases (CLKs) that phosphorylate splicing factors, against vehicle-treated cells [@vangoubergen2024; GEO [GSE259334](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE259334)].
Long reads often span a transcript from end to end, so they assign reads to isoforms with less ambiguity than short reads.
The analysis is the same as for short reads; only the quantification step changes.

## The data

The 6 samples (3 vehicle, 3 lorecivivint) were quantified with Oarfish [@oarfish] against the GENCODE v49 transcripts [@gencode] in its nanopore cDNA mode, with 30 bootstrap replicates per sample; each sample has 6.3 to 7.0 million reads assigned to transcripts.
Transcripts were tested with `swish` [@swish] on the bootstrap replicates and genes with `DESeq2` on the summed counts.
The scripts that download the reads from SRA and run every step are in `data-raw/case_studies/` of the package repository.

The result is an `IsoformicExperiment` saved with `write_isoformic()`.
It keeps the complete differential expression tables (every tested transcript and gene) but the expression assays and exon structures only of a panel of 48 genes, so that it fits in the repository; it is not installed with the package.
`read_oarfish()` creates the same object from the Oarfish output directly, as shown in the [preprocessing article](isoformic-preprocess.html).

```{r}
#| message: false
library(isoformic)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data_dir <- "data/prostate_ont"
iso <- read_isoformic(data_dir)
iso
col_data(iso)
iso@metadata[c("quantification", "transcript_de", "gene_de")]
```

## Checking the samples first

The first principal component of the gene-level counts does not separate the treatments, but the second one does.
With three samples per group there is no sign of a batch to adjust for.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
pca <- read_parquet(fs::path(data_dir, "sample_pca.parquet")) |>
  left_join(col_data(iso), by = "sample_id")
ggplot(pca, aes(PC1, PC2, color = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    x = sprintf("PC1 (%.0f%%)", 100 * pca$var_PC1[1]),
    y = sprintf("PC2 (%.0f%%)", 100 * pca$var_PC2[1])
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Differential expression at two levels

```{r}
deg <- de_gene(iso)
det <- de_tx(iso)
c(
  genes_tested = nrow(deg),
  genes_fdr_5 = sum(deg$qvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
  transcripts_tested = nrow(det),
  transcripts_fdr_5 = sum(det$qvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
)
```

At a false discovery rate of 5%, `DESeq2` finds 140 genes and `swish` 287 transcripts.
`swish` computes its p-values from permutations of the samples, and three against three samples allow only a few distinct permutations: all 287 significant transcripts share the smallest q-value, so they are ranked by fold change below.

```{r}
range(det$qvalue[det$qvalue < 0.05], na.rm = TRUE)
```

Most significant transcripts are protein coding, followed by lncRNAs:

```{r}
det |>
  filter(qvalue < 0.05) |>
  left_join(tx_annot(iso), by = "transcript_id") |>
  count(transcript_type, sort = TRUE)
```

`isoform_switches()` relates the two levels with the default cutoffs of the experiment (an absolute log2 fold change of at least 1 and a false discovery rate below 5%).
Two thirds of the genes with a significant transcript have no significant change of their total expression (`det_not_deg`).

```{r}
switches <- isoform_switches(iso)
table(switches$switch_type)
switches |>
  filter(switch_type == "det_not_deg") |>
  select(gene_name, n_tx_tested, n_det_up, n_det_down, det_sig_types, gene_log2FC) |>
  head(10)
```

## The CLK genes regulate themselves

The CLK genes are among them: lorecivivint raises one protein coding isoform each of *CLK1*, *CLK3* and *CLK4*.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 10
plot_log2fc(iso, feature = c("CLK1", "CLK3", "CLK4"), ncol = 2)
```

The gene-level results show why the classification needs care.
*CLK1* and *CLK3* are significant in `DESeq2`, but their shrunken fold changes (1.8-fold) are below the cutoff of 2-fold, so `isoform_switches()` does not count them as changed genes:

```{r}
deg |>
  left_join(annot_data_genes(iso)[c("gene_id", "gene_name")], by = "gene_id") |>
  filter(gene_name %in% c("CLK1", "CLK3", "CLK4")) |>
  select(gene_name, log2FC, qvalue, deg_sig)
```

The isoforms of *CLK1* explain most of its gene-level change.
`CLK1-201` encodes the full-length kinase; `CLK1-204` is the same transcript without exon 4, which shifts the reading frame and makes it a target of nonsense-mediated decay; `CLK1-210` keeps the introns on both sides of exon 4.
CLK1 activity favours the skipping of its own exon 4, and CLK inhibitors shift the balance towards the full-length isoform [@uzor2018].
The long reads show that shift: the full-length isoform rises from about 17 to 46 transcripts per million while the skipped one falls from about 4 to 1.5 (not significant on its own, with q = 0.25).

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
plot_tx_expr(iso, gene_name = "CLK1", group = "condition")
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 10
plot_genomic_context(iso, gene_name = "CLK1")
```

## The genes of the original study

@vangoubergen2024 report that CLK inhibition lowers the expression of the androgen receptor splice variant ARV7 through the CLK2/SRSF9 axis.
In these three against three nanopore samples, no transcript of *AR*, *CLK2* or *SRSF9* reaches a false discovery rate of 5%; *SRSF3* has one protein coding isoform with a small but significant decrease.

```{r}
det |>
  left_join(tx_annot(iso), by = "transcript_id") |>
  filter(gene_name %in% c("AR", "CLK2", "SRSF9", "SRSF3")) |>
  summarise(
    n_tested = n(),
    best_qvalue = min(qvalue),
    log2FC_of_best = log2FC[which.min(qvalue)],
    .by = gene_name
  )
```

## Enrichment by transcript type

The package directory holds the hallmark gene sets of MSigDB [@msigdb].
`run_enrichment()` ranks the transcripts by fold change and runs the enrichment separately for each group of transcript types.

```{r}
#| warning: false
genesets <- read_gmt(fs::path(data_dir, "genesets.gmt"))
set.seed(42)
enrichment <- run_enrichment(iso, genesets, pval_cutoff = 0.05)
table(enrichment$experiment)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 10
plot_enrichment(enrichment, n = 20)
```

The androgen response, cholesterol homeostasis and mitotic spindle genes go down in the protein coding isoforms of the treated cells, in line with the anti-proliferative effect of lorecivivint reported by @vangoubergen2024.
The proliferation sets (G2M checkpoint, E2F and MYC targets) go down in the retained intron and other unproductive isoforms, but not in the protein coding ones: a part of the response to the drug that only the transcript-level analysis shows.
